publications.explanation: A, self-awareness. The clue is noticing and understanding your own emotions as they arise and change. For example, recognising that you are becoming frustrated is self-awareness; deciding how to respond calmly involves self-management. Self-efficacy concerns belief in your ability to perform a task, self-concept is your broader view of yourself, and self-confidence concerns assurance in yourself. These ideas can overlap, but awareness of emotions is the specific skill asked here. [CASEL, Self-Awareness and Self-Management](https://casel.org/fundamentals-of-sel/what-is-the-casel-framework/).

publications.explanation:
D, all of these, is the intended choice. Closed questions invite a short, specific response, such as yes/no or a selected option. They can help keep an interview focused and gather particular facts quickly. A simple question can also give a hesitant interviewee an easier starting point.

These are possible uses, not guaranteed results: closed questions do not automatically save money or make every shy person talk. Follow with open questions when you need a fuller account; a string of closed questions can restrict dialogue. [Open University, Asking questions](https://www.open.edu/openlearn/education-development/conducting-qualitative-interviews-introduction/content-section-5.1); [MacEwan University, Types of Interview Questions](https://openbooks.macewan.ca/professionalcommunication/chapter/6-8-types-of-interview-questions/).
